name: Helping models know what they don't know
gist: Building systems that estimate how confident they are and admit uncertainty rather than guessing when they're unsure.
explain: A neural network trained to classify images usually gives a confidence score for each class. But this score does not reflect true uncertainty. If the model has never seen an image like the input before, it might still confidently misclassify it. In high-stakes applications — medical diagnosis, autonomous driving, security — confidence without calibration is dangerous. How can you make a vision model admit when it is uncertain, or when the input is far outside its training distribution? How do you know when to trust the model and when to escalate to a human?

The problem is that standard training makes models overconfident. A neural network trained on ImageNet can classify any image — it must pick a label even when none of the labels make sense. A deepfake detector trained on one generation method fails on videos from a newer model, but confidently guesses anyway. Uncertainty is a learned behavior, not automatic. To solve this, researchers use several strategies. Bayesian approaches treat neural network weights as probability distributions, so predictions come with uncertainty intervals. Ensemble methods train multiple models and measure disagreement as uncertainty. Calibration techniques adjust the confidence scores after training so they match true accuracy. Out-of-distribution detection methods learn to spot inputs that are far from the training distribution. Some approaches combine multiple signals: use the network's own confidence, measure input similarity to training data, check for logical consistency, and aggregate these clues.

Papers in this area focus on making vision models more trustworthy. Some develop new architectures that naturally produce calibrated uncertainty. Others propose post-hoc methods that can be applied to any pre-trained model. Some use self-supervised learning on large unlabeled datasets to learn what 'normal' data looks like, so anomalies stand out. Others use test-time approaches: when the model encounters an uncertain case, it can request more information or ask a human. The goal is simple: models that know the limits of their own knowledge and fail gracefully rather than confidently making wrong calls. This matters because wrong confident predictions erode trust faster than honest uncertainty — once users learn a system lies with confidence, they stop using it entirely.

papers.title: CoGe-GCD: Reframing Generalized Category Discovery with Compositional Generalization
papers.contribution: Consistently improves all-class accuracy, unknown-class number estimation, and geometric quality on standard benchmarks with marginal computational overhead.

papers.title: SCalDA: Semantics-Calibrated and Diffusion-Enhanced Data Augmentation
papers.contribution: Achieves consistent improvements for both fine-grained and general image classification tasks through precise guidance across three domains.

papers.title: VGGT-Motion: Motion-Aware Calibration-Free Monocular SLAM for Long-Range Consistency
papers.contribution: Achieves state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot, long-range calibration-free monocular SLAM with markedly improved trajectory accuracy and efficiency over kilometer-scale trajectories.

papers.title: NeuroMamba: A Universal Spatiotemporal Module for Robust Perception in Degraded Sensory Streams
papers.contribution: Reconciles completeness-fidelity trade-off on nuScenes robustness benchmark, outperforming existing approaches in restoring high-fidelity spatiotemporal features from severely degraded observations.
